finding: 1966 LIMMCO catalog is independently documented as a New York-made catalog and is specifically cited in later specialist research as evidence that LIMMCO distributed Hilgen amplifiers. The catalog itself was not retrieved in this pass, so individual pedal listings from it are not treated as verified here.
evidence_summary: The existence of a 1966 LIMMCO Musical Instruments & Accessories catalog is independently indexed; Tone Machines also explicitly refers to a 1966 LIMMCO catalog when discussing Hilgen distribution.

finding: Specialist research places the Kimberly Fuzz Box in 1966 and later tracks a change to the Kimberly Buzz Box and Volume Expander. The exact date of the naming change is still unresolved.
evidence_summary: Tone Machines identifies the Fall 1966 Kimberly Buzz Box and Volume Expander as a new LIMMCO house-brand fuzz; a separate 2025 chronology states the pedal was initially labeled Kimberly Fuzz Box before becoming Kimberly Buzz Box and Volume Expander.

finding: Bob Seidman's account, as reported by Tone Machines, says the Kimberly Buzz Box and Volume Expander was initially made in LIMMCO's Long Island warehouse before the labor burden led to a third-party builder. This is retained as a period production state, not a blanket LIMMCO factory claim for later versions.
evidence_summary: onemachines reports direct owner testimony that initial units were made in the LIMMCO warehouse on Long Island.

finding: Effects Database catalogs a Kimberly Fuzz Box and Volume Expander as v1 by LIMMCO and v2 by Applied; the related Kimberly Buzz Box page repeats the Applied relationship. This supports a distinct Applied-built state after the initial LIMMCO-made version.
evidence_summary: The database explicitly separates LIMMCO v1 and Applied v2 rather than treating all Kimberly fuzzes as one factory state.

finding: The later Kimberly fuzz family is separately linked to UMI products including Apollo No. 843 and Conrad Buzz Box & Volume Expander. Exact transition date from Applied to UMI remains open.
evidence_summary: Effects Database groups Apollo No. 843 and Conrad with the Kimberly family and identifies those as UMI; specialist research says UMI later produced the Kimberly line through the end of the run.

finding: Nomad is documented by specialist research as a LIMMCO house brand. This establishes a marketing/distribution relationship, not a single manufacturing source for all Nomad effects.
evidence_summary: Tone Machines explicitly describes Nomad as a LIMMCO house brand and separately documents Nomad products made by Applied Audio; other Nomad states remain unresolved or UMI-linked.

finding: Bob Seidman is described as an early U.S.-Japan musical-instrument business connector, helping explain why LIMMCO-branded/imported products cannot be assumed to be U.S.-built. This is contextual evidence only, not model-level factory proof.
evidence_summary: Tone Machines' LIMMCO interview article attributes significant U.S.-Japan trade activity to Seidman; the Kimberly instrument line is independently associated with Japanese production and LIMMCO importation.
